newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - March 14.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - March 14.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- N BROWN CONFIRMS FREEMANS TALKS

Mail order group N Brown has confirmed it is in talks to buy Freemans from Sears. Shares in the group were suspended. N Brown is considering paying a similar price -- 395 million stg -- for Freemans as previously agreed by Littlewoods.

The deal is expected to be financed by a rights issue of between 150 million stg and 200 million stg plus borrowings. Chairman Sir David Alliance and his family hold 59 percent of the company's shares and the acquisition is expected to transform the group.
-- SCOTTISH AMICABLE BEGINS COUNTDOWN TO DEADLINE

Scottish Amicable has warned its suitors to place final bids today or miss out on the auction for ownership of the mutual insurer. The successful bidder will pay more than two billion stg. The three bidders are Abbey National, Prudential and Australian Mutual Provident. Scottish Amicable will set up a panel to deal with any disputes that may arise from the bidding process.
-- REDUNDANCY PAYOUTS COST CORDIANT 5.8 MILLION STG

Following the restructuring of advertising agency Cordiant, formally known as Saatchi and Saatchi, 80 employees shared 5.8 million stg of redundancy pay-offs last year, or 70,000 stg each. Chief executive Bob Seelert insisted there had not been any "brutal slashing" of staff costs, and the company ended the year with a small net increase in its workforce to 10,400. Cordiant has just handed out its first payout to shareholders in seven years.
THE TIMES
-- NATWEST SUSPENDS ANOTHER FOUR STAFF

NatWest Markets, the investment banking arm of NatWest Group, has suspended four staff members and cut eight million stg off bonuses. Losses on its derivatives trading book widened to 90 million stg. Chief executive, Martin Owen, has agreed to forgo 200,000 stg of his 500,000 stg performance-related bonus for 1996. NatWest claim that the losses are due to mispricing of interest rate options dating back to 1994.
-- L&G PREPARES FOR PENSION BY PHONE

Chief executive of Legal and General, David Prosser, has said that the company will begin selling pensions by telephone and that the sales were likely to be execution only, with no advice given. Prosser said there will still be a wide range of pensions available for customers who do need advice through independent financial advisers and agencies. The move will raise questions about the way pensions are sold in the wake of the four billion stg mis-selling scandal.
-- LAWSON'S PEP TALK FAILS TO INSPIRE INVESTORS

Fund manager, M&G, which hired former chancellor Lord Lawson for its television advertising campaign on its personal equity plans, has had a poor response to its launch. The company spent two million stg developing the commercials and has raised just 20 million stg from new investors in the High Income Trust, its new Pep this year. This is a very small amount compared to the nine million stg M&G is putting into press and poster campaigns.
THE GUARDIAN
-- FIRE SALE BY A FRENCH BANK COULD SPARK RECORD IRISH BID

Credit Lyonnais, the state-owned French bank, has been forced, by the European Union, to sell its 54 percent stake in Woodchester, the Irish finance and leasing company. Woodchester's share price has risen by 50 percent in the past six months and is likely to lead to a full bid for the company, which would be at 588 million stg and could be a record for the Irish stock exchange.
-- UNITED TAKES THE BISCUIT

United Biscuits reported full-year profits of 24.4 million stg against a 1995 loss of 100.6 million stg. This follows improvements in almost all of its main businesses. Eric Nicoli, chief executive, said the group's new Go-Ahead range of low-fat products had been selling well, whilst sales in Europe had been higher over the second half. He said that for the first time in years all the company's businesses were making a profit.
-- MIRROR CLOUDS CASH-CALL TALK AS RESULTS REFLECT COST OF PRICE WAR

Mirror Group Newspapers have not commented about speculation that it is preparing a 300 million stg cash-raising exercise and considering a bid for Midland Independent Newspapers, the Birmingham-based publishing rival. Year-end figures show the effects of the rise in newsprint costs and the effects of the newspaper price war. James Allwood, finance director, said the Mirror Group had been subject to rumours of a cash call since the company was refloated on the stock market, after the Maxwell controversy.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- FALL IN INFLATION PUTS SPAIN IN PLACE FOR RATE CUT AND EMU

The Bank of Spain is to cut interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point after figures showed a sharp drop in inflation. The new figures raise the chances of Spain meeting the Maastricht criteria and joining EMU. The Maastricht Treaty says that inflation must not be more than 1.5 percentage points above that of the three best-performing countries and an inflation drop in February increases Spain's chances.
-- GRANADA BACKS AWAY FROM BID FOR YORKSHIRE

Granada has ruled itself out of launching a takeover bid for Yorkshire Tyne-Tees. Granada denied it was talking Yorkshire's price lower to secure a cheaper takeover price. This comes just 24 hours before the announcement of full-year figures from United News and Media, another potential bidder for Yorkshire. Speculation also surrounds Yorkshire's intentions towards Laser, the advertising sales business owned by Granada which sells commercial slots for its owner and Yorkshire.
-- GEC AND FIAT TO UNITE IN BID FOR 600 MILLION STG TRAIN ORDER

Fiat and GEC are to announce the formation of a consortium to bid for the 600 million stg contract to build a new generation of tilting trains for the InterCity West Coast line. The contract from Richard Branson's Virgin Rail is expected to create 5,000 new jobs and will lead to lucrative export orders from abroad. The main rival to the consortium is Swedish company AD Tranz.
